Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: Angola's Law 23/11 (Electronic Communications and Information Services) mandates that operators immediately notify the APD (Data Protection Agency) and INACOM in the event of a security breach that compromises the integrity of personal data. This constitutes mandatory breach notification. Law 7/17 also requires operators to implement preventive security measures and incident management plans. The obligation is statutory, not discretionary.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The CMS Expert Guide verifies that Law 23/11 (Electronic Communications and Information Society Services Law), Article 55, requires operators to notify the APD and INACOM immediately of a security breach affecting personal data. A PLMJ note (2024) confirms the APD issued Circular 2/2024 in October 2024 reinforcing this duty and adding a parallel notification requirement under the Networks and Computer Systems Protection Law (Law 7/17), with defined content requirements for notifications. The general Data Protection Law (22/11) itself contains no explicit breach-notification clause (per DLA Piper), but the sector-specific electronic communications and network security legislation makes notification a clear statutory obligation. Score of 3 (Mandatory) is confirmed; year updated to reflect the most recent authoritative confirmation (APD Circular 2/2024).
revised_comments: Angola's Electronic Communications and Information Society Services Law (Law 23/11), Article 55, requires operators to notify the Data Protection Agency (APD) and the communications regulator (INACOM) immediately of any security breach compromising personal data. The Law on the Protection of Networks and Computer Systems (Law 7/17) imposes a parallel obligation to notify the APD of cybersecurity incidents. In October 2024 the APD issued Circular 2/2024 setting out detailed guidelines for reporting cybersecurity accidents and incidents, including the required content of notifications such as the nature of the breach, its likely consequences, and remedial measures taken. Notification is a statutory obligation rather than a discretionary practice.

Definition: Whether national data protection or privacy legislation exists and explicitly covers payment transaction data, including provisions on data collection, storage, sharing, retention, and user rights over their payment data.
Comments: Angola has a general data protection law — Law No. 22/11 of 17 June 2011 (Lei de Proteção de Dados Pessoais). This is an omnibus personal data protection law that establishes the National Data Protection Authority (APD), data processing principles, data subject rights, and penalties. Additional related laws include Law 23/11 (Electronic Communications), Law 7/17 (Network and IT Systems Protection), and Criminal Code provisions. The law is general-purpose and not payment-specific, thus classified as general data protection legislation rather than specific payment data provisions.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Hunton and Caseguard sources verify that Law 22/11 (17 June 2011), Angola's omnibus Personal Data Protection Law, establishes the National Data Protection Authority (APD), core data processing principles (transparency, lawfulness, proportionality, purpose, accuracy, retention limits) and data subject rights of access, rectification, objection and deletion. The law is general-purpose and contains no payment-specific data provisions; the Electronic Communications Law (23/11) and Networks/Systems Protection Law (7/17) add sector-specific security and breach obligations but are likewise not payment-specific. Score of 2 (General Data Protection Legislation) is confirmed; no evidence found of specific payment-data provisions that would justify a score of 3.
revised_comments: Angola's Law No. 22/11 of 17 June 2011 (Lei da Protecção de Dados Pessoais) is a general-purpose omnibus data protection law establishing the National Data Protection Agency (APD), core data processing principles, and data subject rights of access, rectification and deletion. It applies to all data controllers and processors operating in or targeting Angola, including financial and payment service providers, but contains no payment-specific data provisions. Sector legislation, including the Electronic Communications and Information Society Services Law (23/11) and the Law on the Protection of Networks and Computer Systems (7/17), supplements the general framework with security and breach-notification duties, again without payment-specific rules.

Definition: Whether digital payment systems and access points (apps, USSD, agents) are designed to accommodate persons with disabilities (visual, hearing, mobility, cognitive impairments), and disability-disaggregated coverage rates if data available.
Comments: Partial disability access exists. The Kwenda G2P program includes specific provisions: 'For the elderly and disabled, community workers will go to their homes and provide the benefits in person.' USSD-based payment channels (accessible via basic phones without smartphones) are supported by KWiK for populations who cannot use apps. However, no specific evidence of standardised accessibility features (screen readers, Braille, etc.) built into EMIS or Multicaixa platforms. The primary channels (Multicaixa Express app, ATMs) have limited documented accessibility features. Some agent-assisted channels reduce barriers for people with disabilities.
revision_notes: Confirmed, with fresher and more specific evidence than originally cited. Angop (April 2025) and Correio da Kianda (May 2026) reporting on the Kwenda Urbano rollout confirm that beneficiaries with disabilities (blindness, physical disability, albinism, reduced mobility) receive a Multicaixa-linked card loaded with funds plus disability-specific assistive items (wheelchairs, walking frames, canes for the blind), and that people with reduced mobility have benefits delivered to their homes ('humanização do Kwenda'). This extends the original World Bank evidence of home-visit delivery for elderly/disabled beneficiaries and USSD access via KWiK for non-smartphone users. No evidence was found of accessibility features (screen readers, voice interface, tactile/audio ATMs) built into the core digital rails themselves (Multicaixa Express app, ATM network, EMIS). The evidence supports agent-assisted and programme-level accommodation rather than fully accessible digital design, so Partial (2) is confirmed rather than upgraded to Yes (3).
revised_comments: Angola's main digital G2P channel, the Kwenda cash transfer programme, provides partial accessibility accommodations for persons with disabilities. Beneficiaries with disabilities, albinism, chronic illness or reduced mobility receive a Multicaixa-linked payment card together with disability-specific assistive items such as wheelchairs, walking frames and canes, and community workers deliver benefits directly to the homes of elderly or disabled beneficiaries who cannot travel to distribution points. USSD-based channels supported by KWiK extend access to those without smartphones. There is no documented evidence of built-in accessibility features, such as screen readers, voice interfaces or tactile/audio ATMs, within the core digital payment infrastructure (Multicaixa Express app, ATM network), so accommodation is delivered mainly through agent assistance and programme design rather than accessible digital design.
